headline: Ferguson: non-residential sales up 15% on data-centre and infrastructure projects; guidance raised and shares jump 11%
takeaway: Sales rose 9.5% to $9.0 billion with 7% organic growth, led by a 15% rise in non-residential work, and adjusted EPS rose 8% to $3.43, ahead of the $3.29 consensus. Ferguson raised its 2026 sales outlook to about 7% growth after buying FloWorks, and the shares rose 11%.
results: Ferguson Enterprises reported net sales of $9,026 million for the third quarter, up 9.5%, including 7.0% organic growth and the rest from acquisitions. Non-residential sales rose 15% and residential sales 6%. Gross margin was 30.9%, down 0.4 points, and adjusted operating profit rose 8.9% to $962 million, an unchanged adjusted margin of 10.7%.

Adjusted EPS rose 7.9% to $3.43; reported EPS fell 4.9% to $3.08 because of acquisition-related costs. Adjusted EBITDA rose 9% to $1,028 million. After the FloWorks acquisition, which closed on August 31, net debt rose to 1.7 times adjusted EBITDA from 1.0 times a year earlier.

Over nine months sales rose 6.0% to $25.2 billion and adjusted EPS 7.2% to $9.09. The company completed three acquisitions in the quarter and one after it, eleven this year with about $1.5 billion of combined annual revenue, and declared a quarterly dividend of $0.89.
mgmt: Chief executive Kevin Murphy said markets remain mixed but year-to-date performance and the addition of FloWorks allowed Ferguson to raise its guidance. He pointed to water infrastructure, large capital projects, climate and comfort, and ageing and underbuilt housing as long-term growth drivers.

Ferguson now expects 2026 sales growth of about 7%, up from mid-single digits, and an adjusted operating margin of 9.6% to 9.8%, narrowed from 9.5% to 9.8%. Interest expense guidance rose to about $235 million from $200 million to reflect the acquisition debt, and capital spending to about $425 million.
view: Ferguson is the largest distributor of plumbing, heating, cooling and waterworks supplies in North America, and its results are a good read on where construction money is going. The answer this quarter is clear: non-residential up 15%, residential up 6%. The non-residential surge is driven by what management calls large capital projects — data centres, chip and battery factories, LNG terminals and water systems — which need enormous quantities of pipes, valves and fittings and reward a distributor with national scale and project-management expertise.

FloWorks is a logical extension. It supplies valves, pipes and related products to industrial and energy customers, deepening Ferguson’s exposure to exactly the kind of project work that is growing fastest. Eleven acquisitions adding $1.5 billion of revenue in a year is aggressive even by Ferguson’s standards, and leverage rising to 1.7 times is the cost; it remains comfortable, but it is the highest in several years.

The 11% jump says investors had braced for worse. Housing remains soft, gross margin slipped, and the company itself describes markets as mixed. What they got was proof that Ferguson can grow organically at 7% in a flat construction market by taking share and riding the project boom. The shares now trade at around 23 times earnings, a premium to most distributors, justified only if the data-centre and infrastructure cycle lasts several more years. The raised guidance suggests management thinks it will.
watch: Watch the split between non-residential and residential growth, gross margin as price deflation in some commodity products works through, integration of FloWorks, and the first 2027 outlook with fourth-quarter results.
